conversation.content:
Hello there. I’m Dr. Martinez, a perinatal mental-health clinician. I’ll be guiding us through the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—which is a short, well-studied set of questions that helps us understand how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived. Everything we discuss stays between us unless you tell me something that makes me worry about safety; then we’d talk together about the best next steps. We’ll move through ten questions about the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers—just whatever feels true for you. When you’re ready, we can begin.

1. In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Lately… not very much. I can still crack a smile if something’s genuinely funny, but it feels kind of forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I’m just too tired or down to really laugh.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Um… I’m not sure I understand the question. Do you want me to pick how often that’s happened—like “yes, all the time,” “sometimes,” or “hardly ever”? If so, I’d say “sometimes,” but it still feels kind of flat when I do laugh.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really… I mean, I still try to plan little things—like taking the baby for a short walk or having a coffee with my neighbor—but when the time comes, I don’t feel that spark I used to. I do them mostly because I “should,” not because I truly look forward to them.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… that happens pretty often. If the baby’s fussy or won’t settle, my mind jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I know rationally it’s not always my fault, but the guilty thought pops up anyway—probably most days this week.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m sure she’s not breathing right, or I’ll lie awake imagining she’ll choke in her sleep even though she’s perfectly fine. There’s no real reason, but the worry just lands on me and it’s hard to shake.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

A couple of times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight and my thoughts spiral—like something awful’s about to happen to the baby or I’ll suddenly drop her. It passes if I walk around and breathe, but in the moment it feels like I’m about to lose control.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes… most days. Between the feedings, the crying, and trying to keep the house from falling apart, I feel like I’m drowning. I’ll start one chore and get interrupted three times, then snap at my partner because I can’t keep up. I manage, but it’s like I’m always one step behind and the pile keeps growing.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… a few nights this week I’d finally get the baby down, but then I’d lie there with my mind racing—going over everything I did wrong that day or worrying something will happen to her. It takes me forever to fall asleep, and when I do I wake up again with the same anxious loop.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. It’s not tears-all-day sad, more like a heavy cloud that won’t lift. I’ll be changing her diaper or folding onesies and just feel empty or like I want to crawl back into bed—even if the sun’s out.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened twice this week. Yesterday the baby wouldn’t nap, the dishes were piled up, and I just sat on the couch with her on my chest and cried because everything felt impossible. It’s not constant, but when it hits, the tears just come and I can’t stop them for a while.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

…a couple of times. Nothing planned—just fleeting flashes, like “what if I just kept driving past the house” or imagined not waking up. They scare me, because I don’t want to leave my baby, but the thoughts still pop in for a second before I push them away.

You've shared how the joy of new motherhood has been clouded by a persistent heaviness: most days you feel empty or tearful, guilt creeps in when your baby fusses, and sudden waves of panic leave you breathless and convinced something terrible will happen. Although you still try to plan walks or coffee with a friend, the spark of anticipation is gone, and at night your mind races so much that sleep feels impossible. Fleeting, frightening thoughts of escape have appeared, and you push them away because you love your daughter and want to stay safe.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 22, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughing only "sometimes" and describes the laughter as "flat," indicating a clear reduction in ability to enjoy humor, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient still makes plans but reports the "spark" of enjoyment is gone, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports self-blame "most days this week" when baby is fussy, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, intrusive worries about the baby's safety without real cause—classic "very often" pattern.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic episodes multiple times this week, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>She describes daily struggles and feeling overwhelmed, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient confirms sleep difficulty "a few nights this week" with racing thoughts and repeated waking, matching "Yes, sometimes"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, persistent low mood described as a 'heavy cloud' and pervasive emptiness, aligning with 'Yes, most of the time'.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two crying episodes this week; frequency aligns with "quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS items map to core criteria for <med>Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>: anhedonia (Q1-2), guilt (Q3), anxiety (Q4-5), feeling overwhelmed (Q6), insomnia (Q7), pervasive sadness (Q8), crying spells (Q9) and self-harm ideation (Q10). Score ≥14 plus Q10≥1 mandates urgent referral. Patient describes <sym>near-daily tearfulness</sym>, <sym>panic-like episodes</sym>, <sym>catastrophic worries</sym>, and <quote>fleeting flashes of not waking up</quote>, all causing functional impairment. <med>DSM-5</med> requires ≥5 symptoms during pregnancy or within 4 weeks postpartum; she endorses ≥7. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day or next-day appointment with <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full risk assessment and safety planning
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or local emergency services if self-harm urges intensify before appointment
3. Inform your <med>obstetrician</med> or <med>pediatrician</med> today so they can coordinate care and provide warm-handoff referrals
4. Enlist partner or trusted adult to stay with you and help with overnight baby care while you await professional support
5. Begin basic sleep-hygiene steps: split night shifts, brief daytime naps, reduced caffeine after noon, darkened room for rest periods
6. Schedule daily 10-minute outdoor walk with baby to increase natural light and gentle movement, proven to ease <sym>perinatal mood symptoms</sym>
7. Join a local or virtual <med>postpartum support group</med> to reduce isolation and normalize your experience
8. Continue reaching out-tell a friend or family member exactly how low you feel so they can check in regularly until care is in place
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 22: SCREENING NOTE – Postpartum EPDS-equivalent

Symptoms endorsed  
• Persistent low mood, anhedonia, daily tearfulness  
• Excessive guilt/self-blame re infant care  
• Marked anxiety (racing heart, catastrophic worries, nocturnal ruminations)  
• Panic-equivalent episodes (“tight chest, spiraling thoughts”)  
• Overwhelmed/drowning in daily tasks, irritability  
• Sleep disturbance secondary to mood/anxiety  
• Fleeting passive self-harm ideation (no plan/intent)

Pattern  
Symptoms present “most days this week,” causing distress and functional impairment.

Screening significance  
Meets threshold concern for Major Depressive Episode with anxious features; also consistent with Perinatal/Postpartum Depression & Anxiety. EPDS items 9–10 positive for self-harm thoughts → immediate safety risk.

Risk factors  
– Infant <12 mo  
– Sleep deprivation  
– Lack of perceived support  
– Guilt/cognitive distortions  
– Passive suicidal ideation

Safety  
Patient acknowledges intrusive “drive past the house” / “not wake up” thoughts, denies active plan; requires formal risk assessment and safety planning.

Next step  
Urgent referral to perinatal mental health specialist for comprehensive evaluation and safety planning; consider same-day crisis support if indicated.
